title: Directly editing a VLA's weights improved its performance, with no fine-tuning
content:
Directly editing a VLA's weights improved its performance, with no fine-tuning
I ran the π0.5 DROID policy on two manipulation tasks in simulation. Opus 5.5 analysed why it fails at sorting blocks and fixed it by changing its weights directly. No training and no fine-tuning: four attention heads were turned up 3×. Sorting went from 9 to 27 successes out of 30, and a second task the edit was never designed for got better too.
Setup
The policy is the public pi05_droid_jointpos checkpoint, used exactly as released. Both tasks run in Isaac Sim with a Franka arm, a Robotiq gripper and DROID's two cameras, one over the shoulder and one on the wrist. Objects are placed slightly differently in every episode.
“Put the blue blocks in the right bin and the yellow blocks in the left bin.”
- Objects
- 4 blocks, 2 movable bins 10.5 cm tall
- Success
- every block in its own bin
- Time limit
- 120 s
“Put both white cups into the basket.”
- Objects
- 2 cups, a basket, 7 other objects
- Success
- both cups in the basket
- Time limit
- 60 s
The process
- 1Run the original modelon both tasks
- 2Diagnose Task 1watch the failures, measure what goes wrong
- 3Edit the weightsusing Task 1 only
- 4Run the edited modelon both tasks, same 30 placements
The edit was designed using only the colour-sorting task. The cups task played no part in it and was only measured at the end. All before and after results in the Results section come from 30 object placements per task that were not used while designing the edit.
Who did what
- Me
- Set the question, chose the two tasks, decided to focus on sorting, and reviewed the results.
- Opus 5.5
- Watched the failures and found the cause, designed and ran every experiment, chose the four heads, edited the weights, and ran the before and after tests. It made the edit by writing and running code that tried candidate changes and applied the one it chose.
Results
Task 1 · Colour sorting
Task 2 · Cups in basket
This task was not used at all while designing the edit; it was run at the end only to check nothing broke. It improved instead. Cups are carried higher, as with the blocks, and episodes finish sooner. The gain is smaller than on Task 1.
The robot still sometimes picks up a white box instead of a cup; the edit does not change that.
How Opus 5.5 found the fix
The problem: blocks are carried too low
Opus 5.5 first checked whether the model mixes up the colours. It doesn't: when both bins are on the table it puts almost every block in the right one. The real failure is mechanical. The robot carries the block low, the gripper catches the rim of the bin, and the arm drags the whole bin off the table. After that the task can't be finished.
So the fix is simple to state: carry the block higher, without changing how the robot grasps.
The fix: four “lift higher” dials
π0.5 is built from many small parts called attention heads, 288 of them in total. Each one adds its own small contribution to the robot's next move.
- 1Test each headOpus 5.5 turned each head off, then doubled it, and measured one thing: how high the robot carries the block.
- 2Find the dialsFour heads act like a dial. Turn them down and the carry drops; turn them up and it rises. Grasping stays the same.
- 3Turn them upMultiplying all four by 3 raises the carry by about 2.3 cm on average, which lifts most carries clear of the rim. In the full tests no bin was knocked off in 30 episodes.
Measured while designing the edit, on recorded inputs from the original model. The test results are in the Results section above.
This changes 1.57 million of the model's 3.35 billion weights. The edited model is saved as an ordinary checkpoint and runs with the standard code, with no extra hooks at inference. The tests show what these heads do to the robot's movement; why the model computes it this way internally is a separate question.
Where the edit lives in π0.5
π0.5 is two connected transformers. A large one (2B parameters) reads the camera images, the instruction and the robot's joint positions. A small one (300M, the “action expert”) reads what the large one produced and outputs the next second of movement. Each has 18 layers with 8 heads per layer. Two of the edited heads are in each.
Limits
- One scene per task, in simulation. Other scenes and a real robot are untested.
- The edited model sometimes puts a blue block in the wrong bin: 4 blocks across its 3 failed sorting episodes. The original rarely did this while both bins were on the table.
- Opus 5.5 found the heads by testing many candidates against one measurement, not by guessing in one shot.

report.summary: An AI agent diagnosed a robot policy's failure and fixed it by scaling four attention heads 3×, lifting task success from 9/30 to 27/30 without any training.
report.background: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models like π0.5 combine a large vision-language backbone with a smaller "action expert" that outputs motor commands, trained on large robot datasets such as DROID. The standard remedy when such a policy underperforms on a specific task is fine-tuning or collecting more demonstrations — both expensive, and both risky for the model's other skills. Meanwhile, mechanistic interpretability research has shown that individual attention heads often encode surprisingly clean, editable behaviours. This experiment sits at the intersection: instead of retraining, an AI agent (Opus 5.5) ran diagnostic ablations on individual heads, identified four that act as a "carry height" dial, and scaled their outputs. The result was saved as an ordinary checkpoint, meaning the intervention adds no inference-time overhead — a significant practical detail for anyone deploying robot policies on real hardware.
key_points: The failure was mechanical, not semantic: Opus 5.5 first ruled out colour confusion — the robot rarely grasped the wrong block — and found that it carried blocks too low, snagging the bin rim and dragging the bin off the table, making the task unfinishable.

The fix was four attention heads out of 288. By switching each head off and then doubling it while measuring carry height, the agent found four heads that behave like a dial: turning them up raises the carry without changing the grasp itself.

Multiplying all four by 3 raised average carry height by about 2.3 cm, enough to clear the rim. In 30 test episodes no bin was knocked off, versus repeated failures before. Only 1.57 million of 3.35 billion weights changed.

The edit generalised to an untested task: on the cups-in-basket scene, which played no part in designing the edit, performance improved too — cups were carried higher and episodes finished sooner, though gains were smaller and the model still sometimes grabs a white box.

Caveats matter: this is one simulated scene per task with a real robot untested, and the edited model traded away some colour accuracy, placing 4 blocks in the wrong bin across its 3 failed sorting episodes.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this is a concrete demonstration that interpretability can be an engineering tool, not just a research curiosity — an agent autonomously located and edited a behaviour in a frontier-sized policy. For developers, it suggests a cheaper debugging loop: probe individual heads, find the few that control the failing behaviour, and scale them, rather than collecting demonstrations. That could cut the cost of adapting robot policies to new bins, shelves or grippers. For regular users, the near-term signal is reliability: robots that stop knocking over containers are the difference between a demo and a deployed system. The bigger implication — AI agents that debug and patch other AI models — raises obvious questions about validation and oversight.
report.tools: To follow up, look at Physical Intelligence's openpi repository (the π0.5 / π0 checkpoints and DROID policy), and the DROID dataset for reproduction. NVIDIA Isaac Sim for simulation benchmarking, plus LeRobot for policy training and deployment plumbing. For the interpretability side, TransformerLens and nnsight let you hook and scale individual attention heads in PyTorch models, and SAE-based tooling is worth watching as head-level analysis matures.
